subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Qualitative data is best described as:
options: Data in the form of numbers
Data that is always more accurate
questions.explain: Qualitative data is descriptive (words, opinions, photographs), whereas quantitative data is numerical.

questions.q: On a 1:25,000 OS map, two points are 4 cm apart. The real distance is:
questions.explain: At 1:25,000, 1 cm represents 250 m, so 4 cm represents 1,000 m, which is 1 km.

questions.q: In systematic sampling, data is collected:
questions.explain: Systematic sampling takes measurements at fixed, regular intervals, reducing bias from personal choice.

questions.q: Contour lines on an OS map join points of equal:
questions.explain: Contour lines link points of the same height above sea level, showing the shape and steepness of the land.

questions.q: Evaluating fieldwork involves:
options: Identifying limitations and how the investigation could be improved
questions.explain: Evaluation considers the reliability and limitations of the method and suggests improvements for future investigations.

questions.q: A good geographical hypothesis should be:
options: A question with no clear answer
A specific, testable statement that can be proved or disproved
questions.explain: A hypothesis is a precise, testable statement that fieldwork data can either support or reject.

questions.q: The range of a data set is:
options: The difference between the highest and lowest values
questions.explain: The range is found by subtracting the smallest value from the largest, showing how spread out the data is.

questions.q: A pie chart is best used to show:
options: Data by area on a map
Proportions or parts of a whole
questions.explain: Pie charts divide a circle into segments to show how a total is split into proportions.

questions.q: A graph that shows continuous change over time is best presented as a:
questions.explain: Line graphs are ideal for showing how a continuous variable changes over time.

questions.q: A choropleth map uses:
options: Lines joining points of equal height
Shading or colour to show density or value by area
questions.explain: Choropleth maps use graded shading or colour to represent the value or density of a variable across areas.

questions.q: Stratified sampling means:
options: Dividing the population into groups and sampling each in proportion
questions.explain: Stratified sampling splits a population into sub-groups and samples each in proportion to its size to ensure representation.

questions.q: Which is a strength of random sampling?
options: It removes bias from the selection of sites
It focuses only on interesting locations
It is always the quickest method
It guarantees every area is covered evenly
questions.explain: Random sampling avoids personal bias because every point has an equal chance of being selected.

questions.q: The mean of a data set is calculated by:
options: Adding all values and dividing by how many there are
Subtracting the smallest from the largest
questions.explain: The mean (average) is the sum of all values divided by the number of values.

questions.q: A bearing is measured:
questions.explain: A bearing is an angle measured clockwise from north, given as three figures from 000 to 360 degrees.

questions.q: A bar chart is most suitable for showing:
options: Two variables plotted against each other
questions.explain: Bar charts use separate bars to compare amounts across distinct categories.

questions.q: In a four-figure grid reference, the numbers identify:
options: A whole grid square (1 km by 1 km)
questions.explain: A four-figure grid reference locates a whole 1 km grid square, while a six-figure reference pinpoints a position within it.

questions.q: A population pyramid is used to show:
options: The flow of migrants between countries
The age and sex structure of a population
questions.explain: Population pyramids display the proportion of males and females in each age group of a population.

questions.q: In a six-figure grid reference, which is read first?
questions.explain: Grid references are read 'along the corridor then up the stairs' - eastings first, then northings.

questions.q: Which compass direction lies exactly between north and east?
questions.explain: North-east is the intercardinal direction halfway between north and east.

questions.q: Which scale means 1 cm on the map represents 0.5 km on the ground?
questions.explain: On a 1:50,000 map, 1 cm represents 50,000 cm, which is 500 m or 0.5 km.

questions.q: On an OS map, contour lines that are very close together show:
questions.explain: Closely spaced contours mean height changes quickly over a short distance, indicating a steep slope.

questions.q: Quantitative data is best described as:
options: Numerical information that can be measured or counted
questions.explain: Quantitative data consists of numbers, such as measurements or counts, in contrast to descriptive qualitative data.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Geography B (1GB0) specification; Geographical Investigations Fieldwork
